title: Compact embeddings, throughput & routing pilot discovery
topics: vector DB integration and hybrid search
summary: Discovery call for QuantaDocs evaluating Redwood for an embeddings + rerank pilot. Primary concerns: cost vs latency tradeoffs for high QPS, vector DB integration and routing, options for Dedicated or Private (VPC) due to data residency, and feasibility of using compact 256-d embeddings with a reranker for topk accuracy. Agreed next steps: Redwood to share compact embedding benchmark spreadsheet, proposed pilot topology, and security docs; customer to provide sample query distribution and acceptance SLA targets.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-07-21 09:00 PT / 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Patel (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Maya Rodriguez (QuantaDocs - Head of Search), Ethan Park (QuantaDocs - Infra), Jordan Lee (QuantaDocs - Data Scientist)

[00:00] Sofia Patel: hey everyone thanks for joining,uh we'll kick off in a sec, i'm sofia from redwood. we got liam with me who's our se. maya, want to do quick intros?
[00:12] Maya Rodriguez: sure, hi i'm maya, head of search at quantadocs, we run doc search for our enterprise customers, looking to reduce latency and cost on our rerank flow.
[00:20] Ethan Park: ethan here, infra lead, i'm the one worried about sustain qps and VPC networking.
[00:26] Jordan Lee: jordan, data science, i'm focused on retrieval quality and choosing emb dims.
[00:30] Sofia Patel: awesome, thanks. objective for today is to understand your workload and constraints and walk through options — hosted, dedicated, or private — and talk about compact embeddings + rerank pilot.
[00:42] Liam Chen: quick agenda — workload shape, vector DB + routing architecture, perf tradeoffs for 256 vs 512 vs 1536 dims, and recommended pilot topology.
[00:51] Maya Rodriguez: perfect. to start, our current flow: user query -> vector search in our vector DB -> top 200 results -> lightweight reranker (transformer) to get final top 5. We're seeing cost blow up on the reranker when top-200 is large and qps spikes.
[01:10] Jordan Lee: right now embeddings are 768 dims, stored in an in-house Milvus cluster. We're considering smaller embeddings to reduce index size and fanout.
[01:19] Ethan Park: our p95 tail latency budget is 220 ms for search+rerank combined. We hit 450ms during morning spikes.
[01:28] Sofia Patel: got it. when you say 'reranker' is that run in your infra or currently via a cloud function?
[01:33] Maya Rodriguez: currently on-prem functions; but we want to evaluate offloading the rerank to redwood to use model variants and better batching.
[01:41] Liam Chen: okay, that helps. couple of clarifying q's — typical QPS, avg query tokens, and percent of queries that need deep rerank vs shallow?
[01:50] Jordan Lee: baseline 120 qps steady, spikes to 900 qps sustained for 5-10 minutes a day. Avg query length is short, 6-12 tokens. About 80% of queries can do quick heuristic rerank, but 20% need full transformer rerank.
[02:05] Ethan Park: also note we have strict data residency for EU customers — some datasets must stay in VPC region eu-west-1.
[02:12] Sofia Patel: makes sense — we can discuss dedicated capacity in-region or private deployment (VPC) for those. On embedding dims: are you targeting fidelity loss vs cost? What's acceptable drop in MAP/NDCG?
[02:23] Jordan Lee: we can accept up to 3% drop in NDCG if latency+cost improves significantly. We want to test 256d compact embeddings with a stronger reranker on the topk.
[02:32] Liam Chen: that's a common pattern — compact embeddings for retrieval (lower cost, smaller indexes), plus a heavy reranker on the topk to regain quality. Our pilot guidance usually: store 256d in vector DB for initial fanout of 200, then use Redwood hosted rerank for top50 or top100.
[02:47] Maya Rodriguez: question — how does redwood route to vector DB? Do you recommend keeping Milvus or moving to a hosted vector store?
[02:53] Liam Chen: architectural options: 1) keep your Milvus and call it from Redwood (we call it a hybrid setup; Redwood does the embed+rerank and calls your vector DB via private connection), 2) migrate vectors into Redwood Dedicated-backed store or partner vector DBs (we support connectors to Pinecone and others), 3) use Redwood Private with VPC peering for on-prem Milvus. Each has tradeoffs for latency and egress.
[03:13] Ethan Park: egress is a concern. If we host embeddings in Milvus on-prem, and rerank on hosted redwood, we worry about cross‑region traffic and costs.
[03:20] Sofia Patel: yep, that's why Dedicated or Private are options: Dedicated (reserved GPU pools) in your region reduces egress and keeps throughput predictable; Private gives you full control in your VPC so data never leaves.
[03:30] Jordan Lee: for the compact embeddings — how do you recommend training/quantizing? We saw quantized 256d sometimes lose nuances.
[03:36] Liam Chen: two approaches — distillation to 256d embedding model, or PQ/OPQ quantization on 512/768 dims. Distilled 256d tends to be better for semantic alignment if you retrain on your data. Quantization is cheaper but can add noise. For pilot, we can run A/B: distilled 256d vs quantized 512 to compare recall/latency/cost.
[03:54] Maya Rodriguez: can you run throughput numbers? like tokens/sec or embeddings/sec and expected rerank throughput with batching?
[03:59] Liam Chen: rough numbers — on Redwood Dedicated with 8xA100 equiv, you can do ~400-600 reranks per second with efficient batching for small input lengths, and host model 8ms per token with batching. But real numbers depend on sequence lengths and batch formation. For embedding generation, 256d model is cheaper — about 2-3x lower GPU time than 768d.
[04:22] Ethan Park: tail latency again — if we batch aggressively to improve throughput, do we risk violating the 220ms p95?
[04:28] Liam Chen: there's a balancing act: continuous batching improves throughput but adds queuing latency. Redwood's scheduler has latency-aware policies: you can pin a low-latency pool for 10% of traffic and a batched high-throughput pool for the rest. Also, prefix/KV cache helps for repeated queries. If you mark the top 20% as low-latency, we can serve them with small batches and keep p95 within target.
[04:47] Maya Rodriguez: hmm ok. on the vector DB side, if we reduce to 256d, does that change fanout recommendations?
[04:53] Liam Chen: yes — denser spaces change recall per topk. With compact 256d you might need to increase fanout from 200 to 300 to preserve recall, but because the reranker is cheaper when reducing embeddings size you may still save overall cost. We'll show simulated curves in the benchmark spreadsheet.
[05:10] Jordan Lee: also curious about sharded vector DB—we currently shard by customer id and time. How does Redwood's routing handle sharded index top-k across shards?
[05:18] Liam Chen: Redwood supports hybrid fanout: we can fanout to multiple shards and then do lightweight merge on scores before rerank. For high throughput we recommend colocating shards with the rerank pool in the same region to avoid cross-shard cross‑region traffic.
[05:30] Maya Rodriguez: security — we need SOC2 type II, SSO SAML, KMS integration for keys, and audit logs. Do you have those for Private and Dedicated?
[05:39] Sofia Patel: yes — Dedicated and Private have the enterprise compliance add-ons. We have SOC 2 reports, SAML SSO, RBAC, and KMS integrations for Private. We'll include our security pack in the follow-up.
[05:48] Ethan Park: good. another infra Q: when rerank is offloaded to redwood, how do we send candidate features? We need some signals that live in our DB like click score, last_updated.
[05:58] Liam Chen: we support passing structured metadata and features alongside candidate ids — you can send up to N bytes per candidate (we'll include exact limits). The reranker model can accept text + numeric features; you can also use function-calling style structured payloads. There might be a perf hit if payloads are large, but small scalar features are fine.
[06:16] Maya Rodriguez: we also use a custom tokenization pre-processor before embedding; can we keep that in our infra or must we move to Redwood?
[06:23] Sofia Patel: you can keep preproc in your infra and send the precomputed embeddings to Redwood, or call Redwood to run embedding with a custom tokenizer in a private deployment. For pilot, many teams send precomputed embeddings to avoid edge effects.
[06:33] Jordan Lee: ok — let's talk numbers. show me an example calculation for cost/latency if we did 256d + top100 rerank on Dedicated vs hosted.
[06:42] Liam Chen: sure. example scenario: 120 qps baseline, topk fanout 200, top100 rerank for 20% of queries. With 256d embeddings and dedicated reserved pool (mid-sized), we estimate per-month GPU equivalent cost X (we'll include spreadsheet) — hosted per-call cost is higher due to per-token pricing but no infra ops. The main lever is whether you need predictable throughput — Dedicated reduces unit cost if you commit.
[07:02] Ethan Park: and for EU-residency users we'd need dedicated in eu-west-1 or Private — what's the difference on ops, like who manages updates?
[07:10] Sofia Patel: Dedicated is still managed by Redwood but in a region you pick; Private means the control plane is still Redwood but the compute runs in your VPC (customer-managed network) — you get more control and can use your KMS. Private typically requires longer onboarding and an enterprise contract.
[07:23] Maya Rodriguez: onboarding timeline for Private?
[07:25] Sofia Patel: typically 6-10 weeks for Private (networking, certs, HSM/KMS), Dedicated can be as quick as 2-3 weeks for regional provisioning.
[07:33] Jordan Lee: we want a proof-of-concept pilot first to validate recall vs cost. Can we do a 4-week pilot? we want to test distilled 256d + rerank top50 and quantized 512 + rerank top100.
[07:44] Liam Chen: yes — a 4-week pilot is doable. Suggested pilot: Week1 ingest sample vectors / connect Milvus (hybrid), Week2 run A/B workloads from your query traces, Week3 iterate on thresholds and caching, Week4 collect metrics and SLA evaluation. We'll also include a small synthetic stress test to simulate 900 qps spikes.
[07:58] Maya Rodriguez: about metrics — we need token-level cost, end-to-end latency p50/p95, embedding index size, and recall/NDCG.
[08:08] Liam Chen: agreed — Redwood Console will surface token costs, per-route latency, model-level metrics, and we'll instrument reranker accuracy traces.
[08:16] Ethan Park: one more infra nit — how do you handle cold-cache penalties? if many queries are unique we might not benefit from KV caching.
[08:23] Liam Chen: when cache hit rate is low, batching and autoscaling are the primary levers. Redwood also supports prefix/KV caching for repeated contexts; for one-off queries we recommend provisioning headroom in Dedicated or using fallback smaller models to preserve SLAs.
[08:37] Jordan Lee: curious about model variants — can we fallback to a smaller reranker when queue grows?
[08:41] Sofia Patel: yes, Redwood supports automated fallback policies — you can configure gradated fallbacks (smaller model or cached response) if latency thresholds are threatened.
[08:49] Maya Rodriguez: are there known gotchas when integrating with Milvus?
[08:52] Liam Chen: main ones: network topology (ensure low latency between Redwood compute and Milvus), shard topology and fanout, and index type — IVF/HNSW params need tuning per dim. We'll share a checklist for Milvus integration.
[09:03] Ethan Park: do you have references of similar pilots? any customers in regulated space?
[09:07] Sofia Patel: yes, we have a few fintech and health customers on Private and Dedicated; I can share anonymized case studies and a short architecture doc.
[09:15] Maya Rodriguez: ok useful. earlier you mentioned KV cache — is that for LLM context key/value or for retrieval caches?
[09:21] Liam Chen: different caches — KV cache mainly for autoregressive generation speedups; retrieval cache is for frequently requested embedding results. Both can reduce cost, but retrieval cache works best when queries repeat.
[09:30] Jordan Lee: let's talk about expected index sizes — with 10M docs, 256d vs 768d what's ballpark?
[09:35] Liam Chen: ballpark: 10M x 256d floats ~ 10M * 256 * 4 bytes = ~9.5 GB raw (uncompressed); with quantization and index overhead expect 15-20GB. For 768d you'll be ~3x that, so ~45-60GB. So 256d materially reduces storage and I/O for neighbor search.
[09:56] Maya Rodriguez: alright. walk me through the pilot topology you'd recommend for hybrid test (keep Milvus, offload rerank).
[10:02] Liam Chen: recommended hybrid pilot: 1) Keep Milvus as vector store; 2) Redwood SE sets up a dedicated regional cluster (small reserved) to run embedding + rerank; 3) Connect via private peering or VPN; 4) Traffic split: 10% control, 90% baseline; 5) Capture metrics and run spike tests to 900 qps. We'll provide a variant that runs rerank in your VPC if you want Private later.
[10:24] Ethan Park: networking: do you have a template for VPN config and required ports?
[10:29] Sofia Patel: yes, we'll attach a network checklist and port requirements in the security pack.
[10:34] Maya Rodriguez: on pricing — what's the delta between Hosted and Dedicated for steady-state?
[10:39] Sofia Patel: Hosted is usage based — good for small bursts and no ops; Dedicated requires commit but reduces unit cost at scale. We'll send a model cost comparison in the spreadsheet with example numbers tuned to your QPS.
[10:50] Jordan Lee: are you able to run a demo of the reranker with our sample data?
[10:53] Liam Chen: yes, we'd like sample queries and a doc subset; you can anonymize. For demo we'll run A/B comparisons side by side.
[11:00] Maya Rodriguez: ok we'll prepare a 2000-doc export and 500 queries.
[11:05] Sofia Patel: perfect. any other open questions?
[11:09] Ethan Park: maybe licensing — does Private require a different contract?
[11:12] Sofia Patel: yes, Private is enterprise-licensed with longer-term commitment and support terms; Dedicated sits in between. We'll include contract templates.
[11:19] Jordan Lee: last thing — what about feature flags to control fallbacks during the pilot? we need ability to toggle rerank percentage quickly.
[11:25] Liam Chen: Redwood exposes route-level controls and rollout flags; you can change retrain percentage via the console or API and we can automate canary ramping.
[11:33] Maya Rodriguez: great. sounds like we have a path.
[11:36] Sofia Patel: recap / next steps — i'll send the compact embedding benchmark spreadsheet and pilot proposal by 7/23, liam will send recommended batching and KV-cache settings by 7/25, and maya will share query histograms by 7/26. we'll schedule deep dive for week of 7/28.
[11:51] Ethan Park: thanks all.
[11:54] Sofia Patel: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with links to security docs and the checklist. bye.

End of transcript.
notes: Transcript contains occasional mis-transcriptions common to automated call capture (e.g., 'K V cash' for KV cache). Links referenced in call: Compact embedding benchmark (link to spreadsheet), Milvus integration checklist, security pack (SOC2 + network checklist).
